text: Lesson 20 built a workflow that runs dbt build on every pull request. On its own, that workflow running, even failing, doesn't stop anything — a developer could still click Merge on a red X.

The real setting lives in Settings, Branches: a branch protection rule for main, requiring the build-and-test status check specifically. That's what turns the workflow from a report into an actual gate.
Once it's active, the Merge button is disabled on any pull request where build-and-test hasn't passed — not a suggestion, a structural block through GitHub's own interface.
A developer whose change fails a real test sees a red X, a disabled merge button, and a link straight into the failing log — the same log showing exactly which test failed and on which model.

This is the literal mechanism that makes Lesson 1's ask real: not a policy asking people to be careful, but a GitHub setting making a bad merge impossible. Chapter 7 shows exactly this gate catching a real incident.
